newsitem.title: MEXICO: Political fallout could hit Mexico economy -- U.N..
newsitem.headline: Political fallout could hit Mexico economy -- U.N..

text.p: Mexico's mid-term elections this year could have repercussions on the country's financial markets and its fledgling economic recovery, a United Nations commission said in a report.

The report from the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), released in Mexico City, said "non-economic events" had had little impact on Mexican economic activity and financial activities in 1996.
Nonetheless, the report warned "it cannot be ruled out" that this situation will "undergo changes" due to congressional elections set for July 6.
The ECLAC did say, however, that it expected an "unbroken performance" for the economic recovery that began in 1996.
The report drew attention to elections to renew the lower house of Congress and the first-ever election for governor of Mexico City.

Opinion polls and local elections held in November suggest opposition parties could gain considerable ground in Congress from the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has held power since its formation in 1929.
Polls also suggest opposition candidates could win elections for the powerful post of governor of Mexico City.
The ECLAC report agreed with a Mexican Finance Ministry appraisal of the economy and its prospects in 1997.
Mexico's GDP grew 4.5 percent in 1996, after posting its worst recession for half a century in 1995 due to an abrupt and unexpected devaluation of the peso in December 1994.
Economic recovery was driven by exports and "a modest revival" in domestic demand that helped pull employment out of its recent trough but also increased imports, the report said.
ECLAC said Mexico was Latin America's leading exporter, with exports of $95 billion per year, or 38 percent of the regional total and twice those of second-placed Brazil.
The report noted a seasonal spike in inflation for December, due to wages and price increases, but noted the 1996 total of 28 percent was well below 1995 figures of 52 percent.
"Slower inflation is due to exchange rate stability and tight monetary and fiscal policies," the report said.

Nonetheless, the report added that those same policies had jacked up real interest rates and thus increased the financial burden on businesses and families, who had greater difficulty in covering bank debts.
ECLAC noted the peso appreciated by 20 percent in real terms in 1996 due to a trade surplus for the year of $6.292 billion and "substantial flows of foreign direct and portfolio investment."
Finally, the report said total sovereign debt placements of $15 billion in the international markets were "unprecedented."
